messages.author: 71171f0d61fc140f
messages.subject: C++ error when sampling.
parts:
I'm trying to fit a very simple model, just a linear regression. It's estimating two linear functions for the data for two contexts. I've attached my model here, as well as the data, and code to run the model. The model translates to c++ and compiles with no problem, but then when it gets to sampling I get the following error.

Error in sampler$call_sampler(args_list[[i]]) : 
  c++ exception (unknown reason)
error occurred during calling the sampler; sampling not done

I've gone over and over my model, and I just can't find the error. Any help?

-Joe

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: C++ error when sampling.
parts:
On Saturday, June 1, 2013 12:33:40 AM UTC-4, Josef Fruehwald wrote:
I've gone over and over my model, and I just can't find the error. Any help?

If you are going to use uniform(0,100) priors, you need to restrict the support of the corresponding parameters to (0,100).

parameters{
     real alpha[max_context];
     real beta[max_context];
     real<lower=0,upper=100> sigma[max_context];

     matrix<lower=0,upper=100>[max_context, max_speaker] speaker_sigma;
     matrix[max_context, max_speaker] speaker_mu;
}

At which point, you can comment out or otherwise get rid of the uniform priors in the model block.

Ben

messages.author: 71171f0d61fc140f
messages.subject: Re: C++ error when sampling.
parts: Thanks! That did the trick. Frankly, I didn't realize that I could use <lower , upper> restrictions on matrices as well.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: C++ error when sampling.
parts:
On 6/1/13 1:00 AM, Josef Fruehwald wrote:
> Thanks! That did the trick. Frankly, I didn't realize that I could use <lower , upper> restrictions on matrices as well.

We only added this feature fairly recently. The
syntax is rather clunky, but we wanted to keep
size declarations for arrays, matrices and vectors
to a consistent square brackets notation.

The reason you can remove constant uniform distributions for
parameters is that they have implicit uniform distributions
on their declared support.

- Bob
